title: Annual Salary Meaning: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to a Yearly Figure in Australia
description: Understand the annual salary meaning and how to convert hourly pay to a yearly salary using the standard 38-hour week. Includes tax, super, and award rate guidance.

faqs.q: What does annual salary mean in Australia?
faqs.a: Annual salary is the total gross pay you receive in a year before tax and other deductions. It is often expressed as a fixed amount in an employment contract, but it can also be calculated from an hourly rate by multiplying by hours per week and 52 weeks. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that an annualised wage or salary may cover minimum pay, penalties, overtime, allowances, and annual leave loading, provided the employee is not worse off than under the relevant award.

faqs.q: How do I calculate annual salary from my hourly rate?
faqs.a: Use the formula: annual salary ≈ hourly rate × hours per week × 52. For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week at the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour, the annual figure is $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245.44. If you are casual, the rate including 25% loading is $33.05 per hour, giving $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80. Remember that superannuation is paid on top of these amounts.

bodyMarkdown:
## What Does "Annual Salary" Mean?

When you see a job advertisement offering an annual salary, it refers to the total gross pay you would receive over a full year before any deductions such as tax, Medicare levy, or superannuation. In Australia, the term "annual salary" is often used interchangeably with "annualised wage," but there are important legal distinctions. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that an annualised wage is a fixed amount paid each pay period that covers minimum entitlements under an award, such as penalty rates, overtime, and allowances. A salary under an employment contract can also offset these entitlements, provided the employee is not worse off overall.

For most workers, however, the simplest way to understand **annual salary meaning** is as a straightforward calculation: your hourly rate multiplied by the hours you work each week, multiplied by 52 weeks. This is the method used by our [the timesheet](/) and [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tools.

## How to Calculate Annual Pay from an Hourly Rate

The basic formula is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For example, if you earn $30 per hour and work 38 hours per week, your annual salary is $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This figure is your gross income before tax and other deductions.

If you are paid fortnightly, you can also calculate your annual salary by multiplying your fortnightly pay by 26. For instance, a fortnightly pay of $2,280 ($30 × 76 hours) gives the same annual result: $2,280 × 26 = $59,280. Knowing your fortnightly amount is useful for budgeting and comparing with salary offers.

### The 38-Hour Week Assumption

Our calculator assumes a standard 38-hour week, which is the full-time benchmark used by the Fair Work Commission for the National Minimum Wage. If you work fewer or more hours, adjust the formula accordingly. Part-time and casual employees should use their actual weekly hours. The guide reminds employers that they must pay for all time worked, including extra hours, meetings, and compulsory training.

## Minimum Wage, Award Rates, and Casual Loading

Australia has a National Minimum Wage (NMW) that sets the floor for all employees. From 1 July 2026, the NMW is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week. However, most employees are covered by a modern award or enterprise agreement that sets higher minimum rates for their industry or occupation. You can find your award using our [pay guides](/blog) or [reference tables](/data).

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the minimum hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. The casual NMW is therefore $33.05 per hour. When using our calculator, never enter a rate that already includes casual loading; instead, check the "casual loading" checkbox and enter the base rate. Learn more on our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page.

## Superannuation Is Paid on Top

Your annual salary figure does not include superannuation. Under the Super Guarantee, your employer must contribute an additional 12% of your ordinary earnings into a super fund, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 (2026–27). For example, if your annual salary is $80,000, your employer adds $9,600 in super, but that money is not available as take-home pay. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page for more details.

## Tax and the Medicare Levy

Once you have your annual gross salary, you can estimate your tax using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% of excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: $4,020 plus 30% of excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: $31,020 plus 37% of excess over $135,000
- $190,001 and above: $51,370 plus 45% of excess over $190,000

Most residents also pay a Medicare levy of 2% of taxable income. Low-income earners may qualify for a reduction. Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator applies these rates to give you an estimate.

## Important Disclaimer

The annual salary shown on this site is an estimate based on a simple formula: hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For personalised advice, consult the Fair Work Ombudsman or the Australian Taxation Office.
